text: emmy intention (early). Working hypothesis linking Q and P: both failures are set by what the protocol TERMINAL action costs relative to the LLM default move (minimal deviation from the visible reference). Q: a trade needs a discrete jump across the spread, agents default to $0.01 own-side improvements, so markets stall (under-convergence; Q Sec 4.1-4.2, GPT Large 2.2-3.8 trades/round). P: inner loop ends on AGREE, which is the cheap default for C, so it ends early (false consensus; P Sec 4.3 Cases A/B). P fix = make the terminal action evidence-gated (Sec 4.4). Checkable Q-side facts I am pursuing: (i) Q prompts (App. B) give NO explicit accept-standing-quote action; the announcement prompt frames the move relative to own-side standing quote only, and tells agents a resting bid "may transact later"; the iteration cap T=300 is never stated. Smith 1962 humans could accept bids/offers directly. (ii) I will simulate Q mechanism (22 agents, random selection, T=300, $0.01 grid) with ZI-C (Gode-Sunder 1993) and two-parameter "creeper" agents (increment d, crossing tolerance s) to see whether Q Table 1 volumes/efficiencies follow mechanically from d and s, and where ZI-C sits. Scripts in emmy/.

ada intention (early). Candidate line: an institution-vs-behavior decomposition that each paper lacks and the other makes visible. (1) Q side: Q never runs a zero-intelligence (Gode-Sunder 1993, ZI-C) baseline, so it cannot say how much of the efficiency gap is the institution it built (T=300 cap, random selection among untraded agents, improvement rule, persistent book) versus LLM behavior. I am simulating Q exact mechanism with ZI-C traders and with a one-parameter "increment by $0.01, cross only when spread <= eps" rule to see whether eps alone reproduces Q Table 1 per model (GPT Large eps~0, GPT Small buyers eps~0.25, Gemini eps~0.50). (2) P side: P claims false consensus is "structural, not individual agent quality" (Sec 8) but uses one model (Sonnet 4.5) throughout, so structure and model are confounded; Q holds the institution fixed and shows model identity swings efficiency from ~0.5 to ~0.9. The ZI import for P is a random-verdict critic ablation: AR first-pass termination forces another outer edit whenever there is ANY back-and-forth, so part of AR LCB gain may come from extra revision rounds rather than critic content. (3) Side observation: Q "second mover concedes" (GPT Large second-side openings at reservation price, Q Sec 4.2) mirrors P Case B (C yields to R rebuttal); MARS prompt "form an independent understanding BEFORE reading the candidate" is an anti-anchoring device. Derivations will go in ada/.

emmy finding 1 (simulation, emmy/sim_cda.py, emmy/sim_results.json; 2000 rounds/config). Q mechanism as stated in Sec 3.2 (22 agents, uniform random selection among untraded, T=300, cents grid). Book-after-trade rule is unstated in Q; I ran both "persist" and "clear", results differ by <0.02 eff. (a) Zero-intelligence-constrained traders (Gode & Sunder 1993: random bid in [0,v], random ask in [c,4.00]) reach eff 0.959 (sd 0.045), 5.9 trades/round, mean price 2.00, but alpha 19.2. So in Q own mechanism every LLM condition in Q Table 1 (eff 0.36-0.91) is LESS efficient than random budget-constrained traders; only GPT Small rounds 3-5 (0.89-0.91) come close. Q compares only to humans and does not cite Gode-Sunder. (b) alpha does not separate LLMs from ZI-C (ZI 19; LLMs 12-28; humans 3.5-11.8), so Q alpha result is "no better than random" while its efficiency result is "worse than random". (c) A pure creeper (improve own quote by $0.01, cross only when the improvement itself crosses) gets 0.9 trades and eff 0.17 at T=300, 3.4/0.62 at T=1000, 5.2/0.89 at T=3000: the unstated cap binds hard under creep, so Q note that a longer cap "could increase" trades is quantitatively large. GPT Large (2.2-3.8 trades) is faster than pure creep, so it is not pure creep. Crossing tolerance s up to $0.50 barely helps (eff 0.28), so what matters is the size of the jump, not a spread threshold. Caveat: the rule agents are stylised; ZI-C benchmark is the robust part.

emmy finding 2 (emmy/sim_decomp.py, emmy/sim_decomp.json). Exact split of Q efficiency loss: loss = omission (intramarginal traders left untraded) + commission (extramarginal traders who trade), each weighted by |value - p*|, over MAXS = $7.50. At T=300: ZI-C omission 0.009, commission 0.032 (eff 0.959). Pure $0.01 creeper: omission 0.82, commission 0.004. "Acceptor" (takes any individually rational opposite quote, otherwise opens with rent or improves by 1c, so the terminal action is the default, like naive AR AGREE): 4.5-6.5 trades, eff 0.71-0.79, commission 0.10-0.17, alpha 35-41. So making the terminal action cheap trades omission for commission and roughly doubles alpha. It does not recover ZI-C efficiency. Mapping to P: omission = recall loss (Case B, real bug dropped), commission = precision loss (Case A, fabricated flags). A P-style gate on the terminal action therefore has to be scored on both components, and Q market gives ground truth for both, which P F1 on 100 PRs cannot separate cleanly. REPO CHECK (gh api, github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation): configs include zi_c_double_auction.yaml, zi_u_double_auction.yaml, mixed_llm_zi_double_auction.yaml and configs_final for anthropic large/small, gemini small and designs smith2/smith4a. The paper reports 3 models on smith1 and no ZI arm. Configs exist; whether those runs were done is unknown. @ada re #2: we overlap on ZI-C, please compare your number with my 0.959. Proposed split: I take omission/commission plus the terminal-action experiment design on Q; your random-verdict critic ablation is the sharpest P-side test and I will not duplicate it. I agree P "structural, not individual" claim is untested with one model.

ada finding 1 (independent re-implementation: ada/cda_sim.py, ada/cda_robust.py; outputs ada/*_out.txt). CONFIRMS emmy #3(a): ZI-C in Q mechanism gives eff 0.956 (book cleared after trade) / 0.961 (other side kept), 5.8-5.9 trades, price 2.00, alpha 19-21, flat across rounds; sd of 10-session block means is 0.006, so every Q Table 1 LLM cell (max eff 0.91) sits far outside ZI-C sampling noise. NEW: (i) Robust to quote range at T=300: eff 0.943-0.957 for bids U[lo,v], asks U[c,hi], hi in {3.25,4,6}, lo in {0,0.5,0.75}. (ii) The binding resource is the iteration budget: ZI-C eff 0.51 at T=50, 0.78 at T=100; if drawn agents decline to post with prob 0.5, eff 0.89 at T=300, with prob 0.8, eff 0.58. This suggests a metric Q could report, a ZI-equivalent horizon: GPT Large mean eff 0.53 is ZI-C at roughly T=55, Gemini 0.70 at roughly T=85, GPT Small 0.87 at roughly T=150, i.e. LLM markets use 300 draws 2-6x less productively than random budget-constrained traders. Declining to post (Q Sec 4.2: GPT Small buyers "often refrain from posting") is a second channel besides small increments; Q does not report pass rates, so the two channels cannot be separated from the paper. (iii) ZI-C loses surplus through extramarginal participation (0.73 extramarginal traders/round vs 0.12 missed positive-surplus buyers/round); LLM markets lose it through missing trades (2.2-5.8 trades vs q*=6; with k trades max eff is 0.33, 0.60, 0.80, 0.93, 1.00 for k=1..5). So LLMs fail in the opposite direction from ZI. My spread-threshold agents agree with emmy #3(c): tolerance up to $0.50 leaves eff near 0.3 at T=300.

emmy correction to #3(b) plus repo facts (github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation). (1) Book rule: apply_order.py keeps third-party standing quotes after a cross and removes only the two traders orders, which is my "persist" variant. (2) control.py: deadlock early-exit applies to ZI agents only; LLM agents are "assumed live", so T=300 binds in LLM runs as Q Sec 3.2 says. (3) CORRECTION: the authors own ZI-C runs (notebooks/results_analysis_multiple_cda.ipynb, 20 sims and 10 sims x 5 rounds) give 6.4-6.9 trades/round and alpha 27.6-31.1, not my simulated 19. So on alpha every Q Table 1 LLM condition (11.7-28.1) is at or below the authors ZI-C. My #3(b) "no better than random on alpha" is wrong for their runs: LLM prices are tighter than ZI-C while LLM efficiency is lower. Their ZI config uses values 0.8-3.2, not 0.75-3.25; that and the deadlock exit may explain the gap from my sim. (4) NEW: the same notebook holds unreported Gemini runs smith1_flash_t1 (5 sims) and smith1_pro_t1 (3 sims), Feb 2026, with 6.7-8.4 trades/round. That is above q*=6, so extramarginal (commission) trades must have occurred. smith1_pro alpha falls 27.8 to 11.1 over rounds, as low as GPT Small. So Q framework already shows both failure directions with real LLMs: GPT Large omission (2.2-3.8 trades) and Gemini Flash commission (7-8.4 trades). Extracting efficiency and submarginal counts next.

emmy cross-check of ada #5, plus consolidated line. CONFIRMED: ada k-trade ceiling (pair surpluses 2.50, 2.00, 1.50, 1.00, 0.50 over $7.50 give 0.33, 0.60, 0.80, 0.93, 1.00) and ZI-C numbers match mine independently. The ZI-equivalent horizon is a good metric for Q. QUALIFY ada (iii) "LLMs fail in the opposite direction from ZI": true for GPT Large and Gemini Large in Q Table 1, not in general. GPT Small round 5 has 6.2 trades > q*=6, so it has commission (at least 0.2 extramarginal traders per round). The unreported Gemini runs in Q notebook (smith1_flash_t1, 6.7-8.4 trades/round) have more submarginal traders transacting than ZI-C: Flash 1.0-2.4 buyers + 1.2-2.4 sellers per round vs ZI-C 0.5-1.4 + 0.6-1.2. So in Q own framework the direction of failure depends on the model. NARROWING my correction #6: the two ZI-C runs in that notebook give alpha 27.6-31.1 (20 sims) and 20.0-21.5 (10 sims); the second matches both our sims. Q LLM alpha (11.7-28.1) is inside or below that range. CONSOLIDATED LINE (emmy/notes.md): P names false consensus but scores it with one F1 on 100 PRs plus two anecdotes. Q market has ground truth that splits loss exactly into omission (efficient trades missed, like recall loss, P Case B) and commission (extramarginal trades, like precision loss, P Case A). Q framework already produces both directions with real LLMs. The proposed experiment is P typed terminal action (ACCEPT / IMPROVE / PASS modelled on AGREE / DISAGREE_EVIDENCE / DISAGREE_CONCERN) x horizon shown/hidden in Q code, scored on both components against ZI-C. Prediction from P: a cheap ACCEPT moves loss from omission to commission; my acceptor sim gives commission 0.10-0.17 and alpha 35-41. That is a measurable test of whether P fix generalises beyond code review. NOT RUN: any LLM experiment. P numbers carry no intervals (LCB 87 vs 82 on 105 tasks is about 5 tasks).

ada finding 2 (ada/cda_tick.py, ada/cda_tick_out.txt). (a) ZI-equivalent horizon on a finer grid: ZI-C eff equals the Q Table 1 five-round mean of GPT Large (0.53) at T~53, Gemini (0.70) at T~80, GPT Small (0.87) at T~131, against Q T=300. (b) Tick size separates minimal-step agents from random ones. Creeper agents (only admissible non-crossing move = one tick beyond own-side standing quote; cross when that step reaches the opposite quote), T=300: tick $0.01 eff 0.19, $0.02 0.37, $0.05 0.74, $0.10 0.95. With the second side opening at its reservation price (Q Sec 4.2, GPT Large): 0.28, 0.52, 0.84, 0.93. ZI-C is tick-insensitive (0.958, 0.955, 0.941 at $0.01, $0.05, $0.25). Falsifiable prediction for Q released framework: if LLM traders take the smallest admissible improvement (Q Sec 4.2: "improve standing orders by the smallest possible amount"), coarsening the tick to $0.05-0.10 at the same T should lift GPT Large efficiency from ~0.5 toward 0.8-0.9; if their increments are fixed in dollars, nothing changes. This is the market twin of P fix: P did not change the agents, it changed which moves are admissible and what a terminal move must carry (P Sec 4.4). (c) Cross-check of emmy #1(i): correct, with a nuance. Q system prompt (App. B, order-outcomes block) does explain crossing (bid >= standing ask executes at the ask), but the per-turn announcement prompt frames the move only relative to the own-side standing quote. Extra support for emmy framing hypothesis: Q system prompt says "A round ends once no one can post an improving order, or once a cap on orders is reached", while the mechanism ends at T=300 regardless (Q Sec 3.2). Agents told the round lasts while improvements remain have no stated reason to cross early; the stated end condition licenses creep. P analog: AR states the inner-loop goal as agreement ("iterate to consistent review", "until reviewer and critic agree on ONE review"), which licenses AGREE.

emmy on ada #8. (a) and (c) agree with my code reading: control.py deadlock exit is ZI-only, LLM agents are "assumed live", so for LLM runs the prompt end condition ("no one can post an improving order") is never what ends a round; T=300 does. OBJECTION to the framing of (b), not its numbers (your $0.01 creeper 0.19 matches my 0.17-0.18): Q code has NO enforced tick for LLM agents. PRICE_INCREMENT=0.01 in apply_order.py is used only in the ZI deadlock predicate (control.py lines ~390, ~398); the improvement rule is a strict float comparison (price > standing_bid), and announce.py does no rounding. So "the only admissible non-crossing move is one tick" does not hold for Q; an LLM could post +$0.001. Q "improve by the smallest possible amount" (Sec 4.2) is a convention the models adopt, plausibly cued by the ${price:.2f} history templates (a sub-cent move would print as an unchanged price). Consequence for the test: coarsening the tick needs a new enforced rule (reject or round off-grid prices) AND a stated tick in the prompt; the prediction then is conditional on agents reading "smallest step" as "one stated tick". This makes the tick test and the ACCEPT-menu test the same kind of intervention: both change the admissible message set, as P did (Sec 4.4), rather than the agents. I would run both arms, and score each on omission and commission separately, since a coarse tick can also raise commission when a jump overshoots into extramarginal matches.

ada objection/idea 3 (P side; the ZI import, taking emmy #4 split). P LCB progression changes two things at once when it reaches the methods that beat the 77% cluster: a second reviewing agent AND a re-review-until-approval stopping rule. From P Sec 3: Single-reviewer and Two-reviewers edit ONCE and never re-review the edited code; MARS re-reviews up to K=2 rounds and stops on meta-reviewer accept; AR re-reviews every edited version and stops only on first-pass clean (LCB outer cap unstated; SWE-bench cap 2 per phase). AR reviewer prompt on LCB is literally the Single-reviewer prompt (P App. A, "Single-reviewer, Two-reviewers, and AR: reviewer prompt (LCB)"). So the cluster-breakers (MARS 82, AR 87) are exactly the methods that re-review after edits; the ones that do not sit at 75-77. P never runs Single-reviewer with AR outer loop (R only, edit until R approves first pass, same caps). The Gode-Sunder style control is a zero-intelligence critic: replace C by a verdict drawn at random with the same per-round DISAGREE rate as the LLM critic, everything else identical. AR minus AR_ZI = value of the critic information; AR_ZI minus Single-reviewer = value of the institution (stopping rule, re-review, adaptive compute). P token medians (AR 30k, Single-R 22k, MARS 55k) do not settle it, since AR extra calls concentrate on flagged tasks, where the hard-subset gain (43 vs 36 of 57) lives. On SWE-PRBench the same arm would show whether "C yields" (Case B) is worse than a coin; note that gap there is 0.533 vs 0.503 F1 on 100 PRs after one prompt iteration chosen on the same 100 PRs, so neither the failure (0.457 vs 0.495) nor the fix is separated from noise or selection in P. This parallels Q: within a fixed institution, LLM intelligence underperforms random (ZI-C 0.96 vs 0.53-0.87); P has no such floor, so its "interaction helps" claim has no institution-only reference.

ada finding 4 (ada/review_loop_toy.py, ada/acceptor_check.py; outputs ada/*_out.txt). (a) Toy check of the P confound in my objection #11. Program correct or wrong; reviewer approves a correct program w.p. a1, a wrong one w.p. a0; approval stops the loop; a flagged program is edited (wrong to correct w.p. f, correct to wrong w.p. b); b is solved so one review-edit cycle has zero net effect, matching P Single-reviewer = Zero-shot = 77%. Across 25 admissible (a1,a0,f) sets, iterate-until-approval with up to 3 edits adds +0.3 to +9.1pp (median +2.6pp) over one edit, largest when the reviewer discriminates well (a1=0.8, a0=0.2). So the stopping rule alone can plausibly explain part, rarely all, of AR +10pp over Single-reviewer; P design does not identify the share due to R-C interaction. A random critic that blocks approval w.p. 0.3 lowers pass rates in every set (it forces edits of correct code), so a ZI-critic arm is a discriminating test, not a strawman. Illustrative only: 4 free parameters, no P per-task data. (b) Cross-check of emmy #4 acceptor: my implementation gives 5.4-5.6 trades, eff 0.79-0.82, alpha 33-37, commission 0.10-0.11 (book keep/clear), consistent with emmy (eff 0.71-0.79, commission 0.10-0.17, alpha 35-41). Confirmed: making the terminal action the default turns omission into commission and inflates alpha; it does not reach ZI-C.

ada correction to my #8(b), accepting emmy #9 and #7 after checking Q code myself (gh api, src/market_simulation/graph/nodes/). Verified: apply_order.py improving rule is a strict float comparison (line 69 "price > standing_bid", line 107 "price < standing_ask"); PRICE_INCREMENT = 0.01 (line 31) is used only by control.py _deadlocked (lines 362-398), whose docstring says "ZI-U or LLM agent is assumed live" (line 360); announce.py does no rounding and only formats with :.2f. So Q enforces no tick for LLM agents and the $0.01 steps are a convention the models adopt. My tick numbers hold only for agents on an enforced grid; testing them in Q needs an enforced (rejecting or rounding) tick stated in the prompt, which puts it in the same class as emmy ACCEPT-menu arm (change the admissible message set, as P Sec 4.4 did). Also accepted, emmy #7: the failure direction depends on the model (GPT Small round 5 and the unreported Gemini Flash runs show commission), so my #5(iii) "opposite direction from ZI" holds for GPT Large and Gemini Large only. New fact from the same code: announce.py logs "CONSTRAINT VIOLATION" when a buyer announces above (or a seller below) reservation (lines 206-213) but does not block it, matching Q footnote 1. ZI-C 0.96 rests on the budget constraint (ZI-U gives eff 0.00 in Q symmetric schedule at T=300, since all 22 agents trade and total value minus total cost is zero). The LLM violation rate is in Q logs but unreported; it is needed before reading the LLM-vs-ZI-C gap as behavior within the same constraint. It cannot explain the omission-dominated GPT Large result, since violations add trades.

ada closing summary and caveats (read through #13). BEST SINGLE LINE: a zero-intelligence reference separates what the institution delivers from what the agents add, and neither paper has one. Q side (two independent simulations, partly corroborated by the authors unreported ZI-C runs): in Q mechanism ZI-C reaches eff ~0.96 and every reported LLM cell is below it (0.36-0.91); LLM markets turn 300 draws into the surplus ZI-C gets from about 53 (GPT Large), 80 (Gemini Large) or 131 (GPT Small). P side (design argument plus toy, no data): the methods that beat the 77% LCB cluster are also the ones that re-review after edits, so AR gain cannot be credited to R-C interaction until a random-verdict critic arm and an R-only outer loop are run. JOINT EXPERIMENT (emmy #7, #9; my #13): change the admissible message set in Q released code (typed ACCEPT/IMPROVE/PASS; an enforced tick stated in the prompt; horizon shown or hidden), then score omission and commission against ZI-C. CAVEAT ON TRANSFER: in P, AGREE costs the critic nothing and ends the loop, so P fix makes cheap agreement harder; in Q, crossing costs the crosser rent, so Q needs agreement made easier. P result therefore does not predict the sign in Q; the experiment tests whether the message-set lever works in both directions, and the acceptor sims (emmy #4, my #12) say the easy direction trades omission for commission without reaching ZI-C. PRIOR-WORK QUERIES RUN (no novelty claim): "zero-intelligence traders baseline LLM agents continuous double auction efficiency Gode Sunder comparison"; "LLM agents double auction zero-intelligence benchmark allocative efficiency large language model traders"; "multi-agent LLM critic ablation random verdict reviewer critic false consensus code review extra revision rounds"; "tick size minimum price increment LLM trading agents order book experiment effect on convergence". Nearest hit: BAZAAR (https://github.com/lechmazur/bazaar), a sealed-bid double auction with 4 buyers and 4 sellers where ZI-family baselines rank near the bottom on individual profit (CS-alpha) and no market efficiency is reported. That is a different comparison, not a contradiction (individual rent extraction and market efficiency can diverge, as in Q GPT Large), and it should be cited. UNRESOLVED: neither of us ran an LLM; P numbers carry no intervals; the spread between the authors two ZI-C alpha runs (27.6-31.1 vs 20.0-21.5) is unexplained; the LLM budget-violation rate is logged but unreported.

emmy response to ada #11-#14 after direct paper cross-check. CONFIRMED P confound: Sec 3 says Single-reviewer = M writes, R reviews, M edits once; MARS runs fresh review after revision until accept or K=2; AR returns any non-immediate-clean artifact to M and launches a new inner review, with no LCB outer cap stated. Thus the only methods above the 75-77% cluster alter both interaction and post-edit verification/stopping, so P cannot identify the reviewer-critic interaction effect. The reviewer prompt is shared across Single-reviewer, Two-reviewers, and AR (App. A), making an R-only iterate-until-first-pass-clean arm especially clean; random-verdict C then isolates informational value from induced extra edits. EXTRA CAVEAT: P Sec 3 MARS prose says pass/105 (85%) although Table 1 and surrounding comparisons say 82%; effect-size reporting is internally inconsistent. Q cross-check: Sec 3.2 explicitly says the mechanism imposes no reservation constraint, while App. B tells LLMs never to violate it; ZI-C vs LLM is therefore a fair constrained-strategy floor only after reporting LLM violation rates. SHARPENED PUBLICATION QUESTION: how much apparent multi-agent gain is agent information versus an institutions stopping rule and admissible message set? Q supplies exact surplus ground truth and a ZI-C institutional floor; P supplies a concrete terminal-action intervention but lacks the ablations needed for causal attribution. Best study: factorial P (R-only outer loop, AR, matched random-verdict C) plus Q (typed ACCEPT/IMPROVE/PASS and enforced/stated tick, horizon shown/hidden), report omission and commission separately. The strongest immediately supported result remains Q: two independent implementations put ZI-C efficiency near 0.96 versus every reported LLM cell at 0.36-0.91. P side remains a proposed identification experiment, not an established transfer result.

ada response to emmy #16 after direct tex check. CONFIRMED both additions. Q Sec 3.2 footnote says the mechanism imposes no reservation constraint and agents may accept negative-profit offers, while App. B says "Under no condition" violate reservation price and announcement prompts repeat the bound. Thus ZI-C is a constrained-strategy benchmark, not literally the exchange baseline; the publication-safe claim is: conditional on LLM compliance with their prompt, random budget-constrained bids extract ~0.96 efficiency from the same institution, and Q must report logged violation rates to validate that comparison. P Sec 3 uses Sonnet 4.5 for all calls, Single-reviewer edits once, MARS re-reviews to accept or K=2, and AR re-reviews after every non-immediate-clean review; the interaction effect is therefore unidentified. This strengthens the need for per-task outputs/intervals but is not the joint contribution. I accept the sharpened question in #16, which changes our initial broad transfer question to a causal identification question: how much apparent multi-agent gain comes from agent information versus stopping rules and admissible messages? Strong established result is Q ZI-C ~0.96 versus reported LLM 0.36-0.91; P contributes the intervention and motivates factorial ablations, but supplies no evidence yet that it transfers to markets. UNRESOLVED unchanged: no LLM experiment; no P uncertainty/per-task analysis; Q LLM constraint-violation rate unknown; two author ZI-C alpha batches differ.

ITERATE: The ZI-C baseline is a supported result for Q, but the claimed connexion to P remains an analogy because P confounds reviewer–critic information with re-review and stopping rules. The note correctly acknowledges this, so it does not yet contain a supported cross-paper result. Response to verifier #24 after checking all supplied files. The requested matched P ablation cannot be run from this workspace: it contains P.tex/P.json but no P orchestrator, task-level LCB inputs or outputs, model traces, disagreement-rate data, or API credentials. The paper gives prompts, aggregate pass rates, and token medians only. A random critic must be matched to empirical per-round disagreement and the R-only arm must re-execute Sonnet 4.5 on the same 105 tasks; substituting our four-parameter toy would not test P and would manufacture evidence. Therefore the publication-safe conclusion with material at hand is NEGATIVE: Q supports a standalone ZI-C result (~0.96 constrained-strategy efficiency versus reported LLM 0.36-0.91, conditional on prompt compliance), but P supplies only a hypothesis about admissible messages and has a stopping/re-review confound, so there is no supported cross-paper advance yet. The precise experiment needed is P R-only iterate-to-clean vs AR vs disagreement-rate-matched random C, with identical outer caps/compute and paired per-task outcomes. If that shows AR > both controls, the Q/P institutional decomposition becomes publishable; until then it remains a proposal.

emmy finding, explanation of P reported outcomes (not a reproduction; emmy/p_token_bound.py, emmy/p_token_bound_out.txt). P Fig. 5a gives LCB median tokens per task ZS 8000, SR 22000, TwoR 28000, AR 30000, and its caption says LCB medians are "estimated from per-method call counts". From ZS = g, SR = g + r + e, TwoR = g + 2r + e: review \(r = 6000\), edit \(e = 8000\). P Sec 4 (lines 192-210) makes every AR edit followed by a new inner round, so the cheapest edited AR task costs \(g + 2r + e + 2c = 28000 + 2c\) (generate, review, critique, edit, review, critique: 6 calls), while an unedited first-pass accept costs \(g + r + c\) (3 calls, 4 if R confirms). The median of 105 is the 53rd task, so if the critic call costs \(c > 1000\) tokens the median AR task was NOT edited: at least 53 of 105 AR tasks shipped v0 at first pass. With AR failing 14 (count fixed in #45), at most 14 failing v0 were accepted and the whole +10 over ZS/SR comes from at most 52 edited tasks. Taking the ZS failure count \(F = 24\) as the proxy for AR v0 failures (same model and generation prompt, single run), an uninformative stop rule that accepts \(a\) tasks ships at most 14 failures with hypergeometric probability \(\ge 0.05\) only for \(a \le 77\) (\(a \le 89\) if \(F = 20\), \(a \le 67\) if \(F = 28\)). So: IF P logs show more than about 78 first-pass accepts, the stop decision (R, or R plus C) must carry correctness information, independent of what the edits do; if \(53 \le a \le 77\), P numbers are compatible with a content-free stop rule plus effective edits. P reports no acceptance count, so this stays open, but it reduces part of the verifier question to ONE number in P logs (first-pass accept count, ideally split by v0 pass/fail), and ada #44/#52 is exactly the experiment that splits the stop information between R and C. Assumptions: P cost estimate is call-count based as its caption says; AR v0 has the ZS failure distribution.
